Asymmetric breath sounds, hyperresonance on percussion, new or worsening hypoxia, or chest imaging showing pleural line with absent peripheral markings or lung collapse — supports pneumothorax (or tension physiology) and helps distinguish from isolated bony injury or aortic injury.

Chest x‑ray showing widened mediastinum, obscured aortic knob, left apical cap, large left hemothorax, or CT/CTA demonstrating mediastinal hematoma/intimal flap — supports traumatic aortic injury and helps prioritize emergent vascular imaging/intervention over isolated chest wall management.

ECG changes (new arrhythmia, conduction block, ischemic changes), elevated serial troponin, or transthoracic echocardiogram showing new wall‑motion abnormality or pericardial effusion — would favor blunt cardiac injury and help separate cardiac contusion from purely thoracic skeletal or vascular injuries.
